# Task: Reverse the cube's rotation with Space

The scene Demo shows a cube named Cube that rotates about the Y axis at 0.7 radians per second. A small red sphere named Marker sits on the cube's +Z face and turns with it.
Change the program so that the cube reverses its rotation direction each time Space is pressed: the first press makes it turn the other way, the second press makes it turn the original way again, and so on. The rotation speed (0.7 radians per second) and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Cube, Demo.Cube.Marker

scene Demo {
    clear_color: #202020;
    state speed: f32 = 0.7;
    state angle: f32 = 0.0;

    camera Main {
        position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 6.0);
        target: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    }

    entity Cube {
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) };
        material: Unlit { color: #6b5cff };

        entity Marker {
            position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.75);
            mesh: Sphere { radius: 0.15 };
            material: Unlit { color: #ef4444 };
        }
    }

    update(dt: f32) {
        angle += speed * dt;
        Cube.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), angle);
    }
}
```

# Task: Reverse the cube's rotation with Space

The scene Demo shows a cube named Cube that rotates about the Y axis at 0.7 radians per second. A small red sphere named Marker sits on the cube's +Z face and turns with it.
Change the program so that the cube reverses its rotation direction each time Space is pressed: the first press makes it turn the other way, the second press makes it turn the original way again, and so on. The rotation speed (0.7 radians per second) and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Cube, Demo.Cube.Marker

messages.content:
# Task: Move a handle along a track with the arrow keys, within limits

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. It shows a thin grey track and, on it, a yellow square block named Handle (#ffd24a) that rests at the centre of the track, at x = 0. One world unit is ten pixels.
Make the Handle respond to the keyboard:
- Each press of the Right arrow key moves the Handle exactly one world unit to the right (+X); each press of the Left arrow key moves it one unit to the left. One press is one move.
- The Handle never leaves the range x = -4 to x = 4: a press that would take it past an end leaves it where it is.
- While the Handle is at either end of that range (x = -4 or x = 4) it is red (#ef4444); at every other position it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- A press of the Enter key puts the Handle back at the centre (x = 0), yellow.
Without any key press nothing moves. The track, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Handle, Demo.Track

# Task: Two lamps: toggle each one, flip both, switch both off

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. It shows two square lamps, LampA on the left and LampB on the right. A lamp is either off (dark grey, #3a3a3a) or on (yellow, #ffd24a). Both lamps start off.
Make the keyboard control the lamps:
- A press of the A key toggles LampA (off becomes on, on becomes off). A press of the B key toggles LampB.

- A press of the Enter key switches both lamps off.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed at the same moment (in the same frame). Without any key press nothing changes. The lamps' shapes and positions, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

messages.content:
# Task: Two lamps: toggle each one, flip both, switch both off

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. It shows two square lamps, LampA on the left and LampB on the right. A lamp is either off (dark grey, #3a3a3a) or on (yellow, #ffd24a). Both lamps start off.
Make the keyboard control the lamps:
- A press of the A key toggles LampA (off becomes on, on becomes off). A press of the B key toggles LampB.
- A press of the Space bar flips both lamps, each from its own state: a lamp that is on goes off and a lamp that is off goes on. (If the lamps are in different states they are still in different states afterwards.)
- A press of the Enter key switches both lamps off.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed at the same moment (in the same frame). Without any key press nothing changes. The lamps' shapes and positions, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampA, Demo.LampB

messages.content:
# Task: Two lamps: toggle each one, flip both, switch both off

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. It shows two square lamps, LampA on the left and LampB on the right. A lamp is either off (dark grey, #3a3a3a) or on (yellow, #ffd24a). Both lamps start off.
Make the keyboard control the lamps:
- A press of the A key toggles LampA (off becomes on, on becomes off). A press of the B key toggles LampB.
- A press of the Space bar flips both lamps, each from its own state: a lamp that is on goes off and a lamp that is off goes on. (If the lamps are in different states they are still in different states afterwards.)
- A press of the Enter key switches both lamps off.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed at the same moment (in the same frame). Without any key press nothing changes. The lamps' shapes and positions, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.LampA, Demo.LampB

# Task: A beacon that runs for 1.5 seconds after Space

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. In the middle it shows a square block named Beacon. The Beacon is always in one of three states, which its colour shows: idle (dark grey, #3a3a3a), running (amber, #ffb000) and done (green, #22c55e). It starts idle.
Make it behave like this:
- A press of the Space bar while the Beacon is idle starts a run: the Beacon turns amber and, after exactly 1.5 seconds of program time, turns green by itself. Program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the run must not depend on how many frames make up those 1.5 seconds.
- A press of the Space bar while the Beacon is running does nothing: the run neither stops nor restarts.
- A press of the Space bar while the Beacon is done sets it back to idle at once.
Every run counts the full 1.5 seconds from its own start. Without any key press nothing changes. The block's size and position, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Beacon

messages.content:
# Task: A marker that follows a position set by the host page, kept inside the panel

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a square grey panel named Panel that spans x and y from -5 to 5, and a small blue block named Marker (1 by 1 world units, #38bdf8) at the panel's centre.
The host page must be able to place the Marker through an input named cursor whose value is a pair of numbers [x, y], a position in world units. Make the Marker follow it:
- When the host sets cursor to [x, y], the Marker moves to x and y (it stays at z = 0).
- The Marker must stay entirely on the panel, so each coordinate is limited on its own to the range -4.5 to 4.5: a coordinate beyond that range becomes the nearest end of the range, the other coordinate is not changed (cursor [9, 1] puts the Marker at x = 4.5, y = 1).
- A press of the Space bar puts the Marker back at the centre (0, 0); the host's next value moves it again.
Before the host sets anything the Marker is at the centre. The panel, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Marker, Demo.Panel

# Task: A marker that follows a position set by the host page, kept inside the panel

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a square grey panel named Panel that spans x and y from -5 to 5, and a small blue block named Marker (1 by 1 world units, #38bdf8) at the panel's centre.
The host page must be able to place the Marker through an input named cursor whose value is a pair of numbers [x, y], a position in world units. Make the Marker follow it:
- When the host sets cursor to [x, y], the Marker moves to x and y (it stays at z = 0).
- The Marker must stay entirely on the panel, so each coordinate is limited on its own to the range -4.5 to 4.5: a coordinate beyond that range becomes the nearest end of the range, the other coordinate is not changed (cursor [9, 1] puts the Marker at x = 4.5, y = 1).
- A press of the Space bar puts the Marker back at the centre (0, 0); the host's next value moves it again.
Before the host sets anything the Marker is at the centre. The panel, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

messages.content:
# Task: A marker that follows a position set by the host page, kept inside the panel

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a square grey panel named Panel that spans x and y from -5 to 5, and a small blue block named Marker (1 by 1 world units, #38bdf8) at the panel's centre.
The host page must be able to place the Marker through an input named cursor whose value is a pair of numbers [x, y], a position in world units. Make the Marker follow it:
- When the host sets cursor to [x, y], the Marker moves to x and y (it stays at z = 0).
- The Marker must stay entirely on the panel, so each coordinate is limited on its own to the range -4.5 to 4.5: a coordinate beyond that range becomes the nearest end of the range, the other coordinate is not changed (cursor [9, 1] puts the Marker at x = 4.5, y = 1).
- A press of the Space bar puts the Marker back at the centre (0, 0); the host's next value moves it again.
Before the host sets anything the Marker is at the centre. The panel, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Marker, Demo.Panel

messages.content:
# Task: Keys that change a counter: double, add three, reset, with a cap

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. A horizontal bar named Bar shows a whole-number counter called value: the bar is value world units long and its left end always stays at the same place. The counter starts at 1, the scene already draws the bar from it, and no key changes the counter yet.
Make these keys change value:
- A press of D doubles it.
- A press of P adds 3 to it.
- A press of R sets it back to 1.
- value never exceeds 8: any result above 8 becomes 8.
Every key press counts and is applied in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, starting from 1, D then P gives (1 x 2) + 3 = 5, while P then D gives (1 + 3) x 2 = 8. Without any key press nothing changes. The bar's drawing, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Bar, Demo.value

# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

messages.content:
# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

messages.content:
# Task: Add and remove pips in a row with the keyboard

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera; one world unit is ten pixels. It shows a thin grey rail named Rail. The program also defines Pip, a reusable description of one small sky-blue block (0.8 by 0.8 world units, #38bdf8) that takes its horizontal position x as an input and sits at (x, 0, 0). No Pip exists at the start: Pips are created and removed while the program runs.
Make the keyboard fill and empty a row of Pips:
- A press of the Space bar adds a Pip at the next free place: the n-th Pip that currently exists is at x = -6 + 2n, so the places are x = -4, -2, 0, 2 and 4, in that order. At most five Pips exist: a press of Space while five exist does nothing.
- A press of the Backspace key removes the most recently added Pip (the one furthest right); with no Pip it does nothing. A place that was emptied is free again.
- A press of the Enter key removes all Pips.
Every key press counts and takes effect in the order the presses were made, also when several keys are pressed in the same frame. A removed Pip leaves nothing behind in the picture. The rail, the definition of Pip, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Pip, Demo.Rail

# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Runner, Demo.Track

# Task: A runner that Space starts and stops and that wraps around

Build a scene named Demo that looks and behaves as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 10) looking at the origin, with an orthographic projection whose visible height is 12.8 world units (near plane 0.1, far plane 1000); so one world unit is ten pixels.
- A thin dark grey track named Track: a box 12 wide, 0.2 high and 0.2 deep at (0, -1, 0), colour #404040.
- An orange block named Runner: a box 1 wide, 1 high and 0.5 deep, colour #f97316, starting at (-5, 0, 0). It starts stopped.
- A press of the Space bar toggles the Runner between stopped and moving. While it is moving it moves along +X at 4 world units per second of program time (program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given; the distance covered in a frame is 4 times that frame's duration). While it is stopped it stays where it is, and starting it again continues from there.
- The Runner's x is kept in the range -6 <= x < 6: when moving takes it to 6 or beyond, 12 is subtracted, so it re-enters at the left.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting). Nothing else moves.

These objects must exist when you are done, each with a three.js `name` (or material `name`) equal to the identifier: Runner, Track

# Reference documentation (three.js r186 and the project's support module)

# Reference: three.js r186 (WebGPU, TSL) and the project's support module

This document is the same for every task. It lists the API a project can rely on; every name in it was checked
against the installed packages (three 0.186.1).

## How a project works

The project is TypeScript (`strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) with one entry, `src/main.ts`, bundled for a browser.
It imports three.js from `three/webgpu` (all classes) and `three/tsl` (the node shading language) and the support module
from `@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`. The entry calls `startTask` exactly once:

```ts
import { Scene } from "three/webgpu";
import { boxMesh, lookAtCamera, startTask, unlit } from "@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support";

void startTask((host) => {
  const scene = new Scene();
  const cube = boxMesh([1, 1, 1], unlit("#22c55e"));
  cube.name = "Cube";
  scene.add(cube);
  host.onKeyDown("Space", () => { /* runs in the input phase of the next frame */ });
  return {
    scene,
    camera: lookAtCamera({ position: [0, 0, 6], target: [0, 0, 0] }),
    clearColor: "#202020",
    update(dt) { cube.rotation.y += dt; },
  };
});
```

`startTask` owns the renderer, a square 128 x 128 sRGB render target and the clock. Tests drive the application
frame by frame; the picture they read is the render target. A frame runs in this order: host inputs, key
transitions (down/up handlers), fixed ticks (`fixedUpdate`, 0 to 4 per frame of 1/60 s each), `update(dt)`, then the
render. Keys are named by `KeyboardEvent.code` (`"Space"`, `"KeyA"`, `"Enter"`, `"ArrowLeft"`).

Objects the task names are found by their `name` property (`mesh.name = "Cube"`, `material.name = "Sweep"`); give each
named thing exactly the name the task uses.

## The support module (`@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`)

```ts
type Vec3 = readonly [number, number, number];
function srgb(hex: string): Color;                       // "#rrggbb" sRGB colour -> three.js linear working colour
function unlit(hex: string): MeshBasicMaterial;          // flat colour, no lighting
function boxMesh(size: Vec3, material: Material): Mesh;  // full edge lengths along x, y, z
function sphereMesh(radius: number, material: Material, segments = 32, rings = 16): Mesh;
function lookAtCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; fovY?: number /* radians, full vertical, default 0.9 */; near?: number /* 0.1 */; far?: number /* 1000 */ }): PerspectiveCamera;  // square aspect
function orthographicCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; height?: number /* visible world height = width, default 10 */; near?: number; far?: number }): OrthographicCamera;
function startTask(build: (host: TaskHost) => TaskApp | Promise<TaskApp>): Promise<void>;

interface TaskHost {
  onKeyDown(code: string, handler: () => void): void;   // after the key went down
  onKeyUp(code: string, handler: () => void): void;     // after the key went up
  isKeyDown(code: string): boolean;                     // as of the current frame
  onInput(name: string, handler: (value: unknown) => void): void; // declares a host input; the page sets it, the handler gets the value in the next frame's input phase
}
interface TaskApp {
  readonly scene: Scene;
  readonly camera: Camera;
  readonly clearColor: string;                          // "#rrggbb" (sRGB)
  fixedUpdate?(dt: number): void;                       // once per fixed tick, dt = 1/60
  update?(dt: number): void;                            // once per frame, dt in seconds (clamped to 0.1)
}

// Textures (an image the project provides as assets/<name>, loaded before the scene is built):
function loadTexture(url: string, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear" /* default srgb */; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): Promise<Texture>;
function configureTexture<T extends Texture>(texture: T, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear"; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): T;
// build may be async: `void startTask(async (host) => { const t = await loadTexture("assets/swatch.png", { filter: "nearest", wrap: "repeat" }); ... })`
```

The camera helpers and primitives use the defaults above; plain three.js objects work as well.

## three.js r186 essentials

Units are metres and radians; the coordinate system is right-handed with +Y up, the camera looks down -Z until it is
told otherwise; colours given as `"#rrggbb"` or hex numbers are sRGB and are converted to the linear working space
(`new Color(0x22c55e)`, `new Color().setStyle("#22c55e")`, or `srgb("#22c55e")`).

**Scene graph.** `Object3D` (base of `Scene`, `Group`, `Mesh`, lights, cameras): `name`, `position` (`Vector3`: `set(x,y,z)`,
`x`, `y`, `z`), `rotation` (`Euler`, radians, order XYZ: `rotation.y += a`), `quaternion`, `scale` (`Vector3`), `visible`,
`add(...children)`, `remove(...children)`, `children`, `parent`, `getObjectByName(name)`, `traverse(fn)`,
`lookAt(x, y, z)`, `rotateX/Y/Z(angle)`. A child's transform is relative to its parent; `new Group()` is an empty
node used to move several objects together.

**Meshes and geometry.** `new Mesh(geometry, material)`. Geometries (all dimensions are full sizes unless it says radius):
`BoxGeometry(width, height, depth)`, `SphereGeometry(radius, widthSegments = 32, heightSegments = 16)`,
`PlaneGeometry(width, height)` (lies in the XY plane facing +Z; `rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2` lays it flat facing +Y),
`CylinderGeometry(radiusTop, radiusBottom, height, radialSegments)`, `ConeGeometry(radius, height, radialSegments)`,
`CircleGeometry(radius, segments)`, `TorusGeometry(radius, tube, radialSegments, tubularSegments)`.

**Materials.** `MeshBasicMaterial({ color, map?, side? })`: unlit flat colour. `MeshStandardMaterial({ color, roughness,
metalness, map? })`: physically based, needs lights. `material.color` is a `Color` (`material.color.set("#ff0000")`,
`.copy(srgb("#ff0000"))`, `.setRGB(r, g, b)` in linear values); `material.name` is a string; `material.map` a `Texture`;
`material.side` is `FrontSide` (default), `BackSide` or `DoubleSide`. A material is shared by every mesh that uses it.
Changing `color` of a built material takes effect on the next frame; nothing has to be rebuilt.

**Lights** (physical units): `AmbientLight(color, intensity)`; `DirectionalLight(color, intensity)` shines from its
`position` toward its `target` (default the origin); `PointLight(color, intensity, distance = 0, decay = 2)` with
`distance` 0 meaning no range limit; `SpotLight`, `HemisphereLight` exist too. A matte surface of colour `albedo` facing a
point light of intensity `I` at distance `d` (decay 2) has the outgoing radiance `albedo * I / (pi * d * d)`; a surface
facing a directional light of intensity `E` squarely has `albedo * E / pi`; ambient light adds `albedo * intensity / pi`
(each multiplied by the light colour). Lights are `Object3D`s: add them to the scene.

**Cameras.** `PerspectiveCamera(fovDegrees, aspect, near, far)` (field of view in DEGREES, vertical), `OrthographicCamera(left, right,
top, bottom, near, far)`; place with `position.set(...)` and `lookAt(...)`.

**Math.** `Vector3` (`set`, `add`, `sub`, `multiplyScalar`, `length`, `normalize`, `lerp`, `clone`), `Color`, `Euler`,
`Quaternion` (`setFromAxisAngle(axis, angle)`), `MathUtils.degToRad`, `MathUtils.clamp`, `MathUtils.lerp`, `MathUtils.mapLinear`.

## TSL (`three/tsl`): shader logic as node expressions

A node material replaces fixed material parameters by node graphs; the shader is built once when the material is first
used, so animate through uniforms, not by replacing the material.

```ts
import { uniform, vec3, color, mix, sin, positionLocal, uv, texture, float, clamp, smoothstep } from "three/tsl";
import { MeshBasicNodeMaterial, MeshStandardNodeMaterial } from "three/webgpu";

const level = uniform(0.25);                 // a node with a mutable `.value` (number, Color, Vector3, ...)
const material = new MeshBasicNodeMaterial(); // unlit; MeshStandardNodeMaterial for lit materials
material.name = "Shade";
material.colorNode = vec3(level);            // per-pixel colour; the result is displayed as it is
level.value = 0.5;                           // updates the shader's input, no rebuild
```

- Constructors: `float(x)`, `vec2(...)`, `vec3(...)` (`vec3(s)` fills all three), `vec4(...)`, `color(colorOrHex)`.
- Arithmetic on nodes: `a.add(b)`, `a.sub(b)`, `a.mul(b)`, `a.div(b)`, `a.oneMinus()`, `a.negate()`; numbers are accepted
  where a node is expected. Components: `v.x`, `v.y`, `v.z`, `v.xyz`.
- Functions (each also a method): `mix(a, b, t)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `smoothstep(lo, hi, x)`, `step(edge, x)`, `sin`, `cos`,
  `abs`, `pow`, `fract`, `min`, `max`, `length`, `normalize`, `dot`, `saturate`.
- Inputs: `positionLocal` (object-space position of the surface point, a vec3), `positionWorld`, `normalLocal`,
  `normalWorld`, `uv()` (texture coordinates, a vec2), `texture(tex, uv?)` (a sampled vec4), `time` (seconds of the
  renderer's own real-time clock, not of the application's frame clock).
- Node material slots: `colorNode` (base colour; for `MeshBasicNodeMaterial` the final colour), `opacityNode`, `roughnessNode`,
  `metalnessNode`, `emissiveNode` (on `MeshStandardNodeMaterial`).
- `color(c)` makes a colour node from a three.js `Color` (for an sRGB hex colour pass `srgb("#rrggbb")`). Node arithmetic on
  colours is done in linear light, and the result is displayed as it is.
- Conditionals: `select(condition, a, b)`; `If(cond, () => { ... })` inside `Fn(() => { ... })`.

## Conventions of the tests

Tests press keys, set host inputs, step frames of a given duration and compare pixels of the render target with
colours. Nothing else is observable: motion shows as pixels, state shows as colours. A project that does not type-check,
throws on start or writes to the console (errors or warnings) fails.

# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

messages.content:
# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

messages.content:
# Task: A spring-loaded launcher: charge while Space is held, fire when it is released

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A yellow block named Stone (#ffd24a, 2 x 2 units) rests on a thin grey rail with its centre at x = -4. Above it a small block named Power shows a whole-number counter called power: the centre of Power is at x = -5.5 + power. power starts at 0, the scene already draws Power from it, and no key changes power yet.
Make the Space key a spring-loaded launcher:
- While Space is held down the Stone is orange (#ff7a1a); at every other time it is yellow (#ffd24a).
- While Space is held down, each press of the Up arrow key adds 1 to power, up to a maximum of 5. A press of Up while Space is not held does nothing.
- When Space is released the Stone is launched: it moves 2 world units to the right for every point of power, but its centre never goes beyond x = 5 (a launch that would take it further leaves it at x = 5). Then power goes back to 0. A launch with power 0 moves nothing.
- Pressing Space, or releasing Up, does nothing by itself: only the release of Space launches.
Every key press and every key release counts and is handled in the order in which it happened, also when several happen at the same moment (in the same frame). For example, pressing Space, pressing Up and releasing Space within one frame launches the Stone with power 1. Without any key event nothing changes. The rail, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Stone, Demo.Power, Demo.power

# Task: Fly a ship with the arrow keys: it moves in every frame a key is held

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. A blue square block named Ship (#38bdf8, 2 x 2 units) is at the centre, x = 0 and y = 0, on a dark grey square named Field (10 x 10 units, centred on the origin).
Make the arrow keys fly the Ship:
- While the Right arrow key is held down the Ship moves along +X at 8 world units per second of program time: in every frame in which the key is held it moves 8 times that frame's duration. Left moves it along -X, Up along +Y and Down along -Y in the same way. Program time is the sum of the frame durations the program is given, and frame durations vary.
- Keys that are held at the same time all act at the same time: Right and Up together move the Ship diagonally, 8 units per second along each of the two axes; two opposite keys held together cancel each other out.
- A key counts as held in the frame in which its press is handled and in every later frame up to, but not including, the frame in which its release is handled. A key that is pressed and released again within the same frame is not held in any frame, so it moves nothing.
- After every frame the centre of the Ship is limited to x and y between -4 and 4, each axis on its own, so the Ship stays inside the Field.
Without a held key nothing moves. The Field, the camera and everything else stay as they are.

void startTask((host) => {

  ship.name = "Ship";

  const SPEED = 8; // world units per second

  const MAX_POS = 4;

      let dx = 0;
      let dy = 0;

      // Check which arrow keys are held and accumulate movement

      if (host.isKeyDown("ArrowLeft")) {
        dx -= SPEED * dt;

      if (host.isKeyDown("ArrowUp")) {
        dy += SPEED * dt;
      }
      if (host.isKeyDown("ArrowDown")) {
        dy -= SPEED * dt;
      }

      // Apply movement
      ship.position.x += dx;
      ship.position.y += dy;

      ship.position.x = MathUtils.clamp(ship.position.x, MIN_POS, MAX_POS);
      ship.position.y = MathUtils.clamp(ship.position.y, MIN_POS, MAX_POS);

  };
});

# Task: Two clocks: a block that moves per fixed tick and a block that moves per frame time

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. Two blocks of 1 x 1 units stand at the left with their centres at x = -5.5: a red block named Ticker (#ef4444) at y = 3 and a cyan block named Glider (#38bdf8) at y = -3. Neither moves yet.
The program has two clocks:
- Frames. Every frame has a duration, the time since the previous frame; a duration longer than 0.1 s counts as 0.1 s. Program time is the sum of the counted durations.
- Fixed steps. The simulation runs in steps of exactly 1/60 s of program time, one tick per step. In each frame the counted duration is added to whatever is left over from earlier frames, and every whole 1/60 s in that sum is one tick, run in order within that frame, but at most 4 ticks run in one frame. Whole steps beyond the fourth are dropped: they are never run later. What is less than one step is kept for the next frame. For example, starting with nothing left over, a frame of 0.04 s (2.4 steps) runs 2 ticks and keeps 0.4 of a step.
Make both blocks move to the right:
- The Ticker moves 0.1 world unit (one pixel) on every tick.
- The Glider moves 6 world units per second of program time: in every frame it moves 6 times that frame's counted duration.
Neither block moves in any other way. The camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ticker, Demo.Glider

messages.content:
# Task: Two clocks: a block that moves per fixed tick and a block that moves per frame time

The scene Demo is drawn from the front with a flat (orthographic) camera. One world unit is ten pixels. Two blocks of 1 x 1 units stand at the left with their centres at x = -5.5: a red block named Ticker (#ef4444) at y = 3 and a cyan block named Glider (#38bdf8) at y = -3. Neither moves yet.
The program has two clocks:
- Frames. Every frame has a duration, the time since the previous frame; a duration longer than 0.1 s counts as 0.1 s. Program time is the sum of the counted durations.
- Fixed steps. The simulation runs in steps of exactly 1/60 s of program time, one tick per step. In each frame the counted duration is added to whatever is left over from earlier frames, and every whole 1/60 s in that sum is one tick, run in order within that frame, but at most 4 ticks run in one frame. Whole steps beyond the fourth are dropped: they are never run later. What is less than one step is kept for the next frame. For example, starting with nothing left over, a frame of 0.04 s (2.4 steps) runs 2 ticks and keeps 0.4 of a step.
Make both blocks move to the right:
- The Ticker moves 0.1 world unit (one pixel) on every tick.
- The Glider moves 6 world units per second of program time: in every frame it moves 6 times that frame's counted duration.
Neither block moves in any other way. The camera and everything else stay as they are.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Ticker, Demo.Glider

# Task: Repair a program with a malformed number, a missing separator, a misspelled name and a type error

The project is meant to show a scene named Demo with a pink box that swings from side to side and rises when Space is pressed, and it does not build. Repair it without removing anything.
Intended behaviour: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a unit cube named Bob with the flat colour #ec4899 (no lighting). The program keeps the elapsed time in seconds, accumulated from the frame time of every frame, in a variable named elapsed, and the number of Space presses so far, a whole number, in a variable named presses. In every frame Bob is placed at x = 2 * sin(t), where t is the elapsed time in radians, at y = 0.5 for each press so far (0 before the first press) and at z = 0.

# Task: Repair a program with a malformed number, a missing separator, a misspelled name and a type error

The project is meant to show a scene named Demo with a pink box that swings from side to side and rises when Space is pressed, and it does not build. Repair it without removing anything.
Intended behaviour: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a unit cube named Bob with the flat colour #ec4899 (no lighting). The program keeps the elapsed time in seconds, accumulated from the frame time of every frame, in a variable named elapsed, and the number of Space presses so far, a whole number, in a variable named presses. In every frame Bob is placed at x = 2 * sin(t), where t is the elapsed time in radians, at y = 0.5 for each press so far (0 before the first press) and at z = 0.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Bob, Demo.elapsed, Demo.presses

response.text:
Looking at this task, I need to understand what's wrong with the turret rotation.

The intended behavior is:
- Space press turns the Turret 30° to the right (as seen from camera)
- After 3 presses, barrel is at world (2.2, 0, 0)
- After 4 presses, barrel is at (1.905, 0, -1.1)

Let me trace through the math:
- Starting position: barrel at local (0, 0, 2.2), which is world (0, 0, 2.2) - pointing toward camera
- "To the right as seen from camera" means rotating around Y-axis in the negative direction (clockwise when looking from +Z toward origin)
- After 1 press (30°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(30°), 0, 2.2 * cos(30°)) = (1.1, 0, 1.905)
- After 3 presses (90°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(90°), 0, 2.2 * cos(90°)) = (2.2, 0, 0) ✓
- After 4 presses (120°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(120°), 0, 2.2 * cos(120°)) = (1.905, 0, -1.1) ✓

The current code does:
```
heading += STEP_DEGREES;
Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
```

The problem is the negation. For a rotation to the right (clockwise from camera's view, which is negative rotation around Y-axis), when heading is positive and growing, we should apply a negative angle. But the current code negates heading, which means:
- After press 1: `heading = 30`, angle = `-30` (correct, rotates right)
- But the logic is backwards because we're incrementing heading positively

Wait, let me reconsider. The current code negates heading, so it should work correctly for the first rotation... unless the issue is different.

Actually, looking more carefully: the code applies `-heading` in radians directly to `quat.axis_angle`, but `STEP_DEGREES` is in degrees! The `quat.axis_angle` function expects radians, not degrees.

So the fix is to convert degrees to radians using the `radians()` function:

<<<FILE src/main.mtek
<<<SEARCH
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
    }
===
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), radians(-heading));
    }
>>>REPLACE

messages.content:
# Task: Repair a turret that turns by the wrong amount and to the wrong side

The project is meant to show a turret that turns when Space is pressed, and the turret does not end up where it should. Repair it without removing anything.
Intended scene: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a cube named Turret with edge length 2 at the origin, flat colour #6b5cff; a cube named Barrel with edge length 0.8, flat colour #f59e0b, attached to the Turret as its child at the local position (0, 0, 2.2), so that at the start it is between the turret and the camera. All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).
Intended behaviour: every press of Space turns the Turret by a further 30 degrees about the vertical axis (Y), to the right as seen from the camera: the barrel swings from the camera toward the right-hand side of the picture, so that after three presses it is at world (2.2, 0, 0) and after four it is at (1.905, 0, -1.1). The program keeps the heading, which grows by one step with each press, in a variable named heading.

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Turret, Demo.Turret.Barrel, Demo.heading

scene Demo {

    state heading: f32 = 0.0;

            material: Unlit { color: #f59e0b };
        }

Reply with edit blocks.

Looking at this task, I need to understand what's wrong with the turret rotation.

The intended behavior is:
- Space press turns the Turret 30° to the right (as seen from camera)
- After 3 presses, barrel is at world (2.2, 0, 0)
- After 4 presses, barrel is at (1.905, 0, -1.1)

Let me trace through the math:
- Starting position: barrel at local (0, 0, 2.2), which is world (0, 0, 2.2) - pointing toward camera
- "To the right as seen from camera" means rotating around Y-axis in the negative direction (clockwise when looking from +Z toward origin)
- After 1 press (30°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(30°), 0, 2.2 * cos(30°)) = (1.1, 0, 1.905)
- After 3 presses (90°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(90°), 0, 2.2 * cos(90°)) = (2.2, 0, 0) ✓
- After 4 presses (120°): barrel should be at (2.2 * sin(120°), 0, 2.2 * cos(120°)) = (1.905, 0, -1.1) ✓

The current code does:
```
heading += STEP_DEGREES;
Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
```

The problem is the negation. For a rotation to the right (clockwise from camera's view, which is negative rotation around Y-axis), when heading is positive and growing, we should apply a negative angle. But the current code negates heading, which means:
- After press 1: `heading = 30`, angle = `-30` (correct, rotates right)
- But the logic is backwards because we're incrementing heading positively

Wait, let me reconsider. The current code negates heading, so it should work correctly for the first rotation... unless the issue is different.

Actually, looking more carefully: the code applies `-heading` in radians directly to `quat.axis_angle`, but `STEP_DEGREES` is in degrees! The `quat.axis_angle` function expects radians, not degrees.

So the fix is to convert degrees to radians using the `radians()` function:

<<<FILE src/main.mtek
<<<SEARCH
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), -heading);
    }
===
    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        heading += STEP_DEGREES;
        Turret.rotation = quat.axis_angle(vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), radians(-heading));
    }
>>>REPLACE

# Task: Rename the lamp's glow input to brightness without changing its behaviour

The project shows a lamp: a grey housing with a yellow bulb in front of it, and the size of the bulb follows a number called glow. The page that hosts the project is being changed and will from now on call this number brightness; it no longer uses the name glow. Rename it consistently: the variable glow becomes brightness everywhere it is used, and the input through which the page sets it is named brightness (the old input name goes away). Nothing else changes: the lamp looks and behaves exactly as before.
Behaviour that must stay: clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; a box named Housing, 5 x 5 x 1, at the origin with the flat colour #4b5563; a box named Bulb, flat colour #fde047, a square plate in front of the housing at (0, 0, 1) whose edge is 1 + 2 * brightness and whose thickness is 0.2 (so the edge is 2 at the starting brightness of 0.5); pressing Space sets the brightness to 1, pressing D sets it to 0, and the page can set it to any number between 0 and 1. All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Bulb, Demo.Housing

scene Demo {
    clear_color: #202020;
    /// The lamp's brightness from 0.0 (small) to 1.0 (large); the host page sets it.
    state glow: f32 = 0.5;

    camera Main {
        position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 8.0);
        target: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    }

    // The housing never changes.
    entity Housing {
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(5.0, 5.0, 1.0) };
        material: Unlit { color: #4b5563 };
    }

    // The bulb is a square plate in front of the housing; its edge is 1.0 + 2.0 * glow.
    entity Bulb {
        position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
        scale: bind(vec3(0.5 + glow, 0.5 + glow, 1.0));
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(2.0, 2.0, 0.2) };
        material: Unlit { color: #fde047 };
    }

    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        glow = 1.0;
    }

    on key_down(Key.D) {
        glow = 0.0;
    }
}

messages.content:
# Task: Add an alarm lamp and a reset key to a working counter without changing what it does

The project is a counter: five green pips in a row, and every press of Space lights one more pip from the left, never more than five. It works. Extend it with two features without changing anything that already works.
Present behaviour (it must stay): clear colour #202020; one camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin; five boxes named Pip1 to Pip5, edge length 0.7, flat colour #22c55e, at x = -3, -1.5, 0, 1.5 and 3 (y = -2, z = 0); pip number n is visible exactly while the count of presses is at least n; the count is kept in a variable named count and stops at 5 (further presses change nothing); no pip is visible at the start.
New: (1) a box named Alarm, edge length 1, flat colour #ef4444, at (0, 2, 0), that is visible exactly while all five pips are lit and hidden otherwise (so it is hidden at the start); (2) pressing R sets the count back to 0, so that every pip and the alarm are hidden again and counting starts again from the left. All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.count, Demo.Pip1, Demo.Pip2, Demo.Pip3, Demo.Pip4, Demo.Pip5

const MAX_COUNT: i32 = 5;

scene Demo {
    clear_color: #202020;
    // How many pips are lit, from 0 to MAX_COUNT.
    state count: i32 = 0;

    camera Main {
        position: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 8.0);
        target: vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0);
    }

    entity Pip1 {
        position: vec3(-3.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 1);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip2 {
        position: vec3(-1.5, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 2);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip3 {
        position: vec3(0.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 3);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip4 {
        position: vec3(1.5, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 4);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    entity Pip5 {
        position: vec3(3.0, -2.0, 0.0);
        visible: bind(count >= 5);
        mesh: Box { size: vec3(0.7, 0.7, 0.7) };
        material: Unlit { color: #22c55e };
    }

    on key_down(Key.Space) {
        if count < MAX_COUNT {
            count += 1;
        }
    }
}

# Task: A green box and a blue sphere on a dark grey background

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #202020.
- One camera at (0, 0, 6) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.9 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A green box named Cube at the origin: colour #22c55e, edge length 1.0.
- A blue sphere named Ball at (2, 0, 0), that is to the right of the box as seen from the camera: colour #3b82f6, radius 0.5.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These objects must exist when you are done, each with a three.js `name` (or material `name`) equal to the identifier: Cube, Ball

# Reference documentation (three.js r186 and the project's support module)

# Reference: three.js r186 (WebGPU, TSL) and the project's support module

This document is the same for every task. It lists the API a project can rely on; every name in it was checked
against the installed packages (three 0.186.1).

## How a project works

The project is TypeScript (`strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) with one entry, `src/main.ts`, bundled for a browser.
It imports three.js from `three/webgpu` (all classes) and `three/tsl` (the node shading language) and the support module
from `@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`. The entry calls `startTask` exactly once:

```ts
import { Scene } from "three/webgpu";
import { boxMesh, lookAtCamera, startTask, unlit } from "@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support";

void startTask((host) => {
  const scene = new Scene();
  const cube = boxMesh([1, 1, 1], unlit("#22c55e"));
  cube.name = "Cube";
  scene.add(cube);
  host.onKeyDown("Space", () => { /* runs in the input phase of the next frame */ });
  return {
    scene,
    camera: lookAtCamera({ position: [0, 0, 6], target: [0, 0, 0] }),
    clearColor: "#202020",
    update(dt) { cube.rotation.y += dt; },
  };
});
```

`startTask` owns the renderer, a square 128 x 128 sRGB render target and the clock. Tests drive the application
frame by frame; the picture they read is the render target. A frame runs in this order: host inputs, key
transitions (down/up handlers), fixed ticks (`fixedUpdate`, 0 to 4 per frame of 1/60 s each), `update(dt)`, then the
render. Keys are named by `KeyboardEvent.code` (`"Space"`, `"KeyA"`, `"Enter"`, `"ArrowLeft"`).

Objects the task names are found by their `name` property (`mesh.name = "Cube"`, `material.name = "Sweep"`); give each
named thing exactly the name the task uses.

## The support module (`@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`)

```ts
type Vec3 = readonly [number, number, number];
function srgb(hex: string): Color;                       // "#rrggbb" sRGB colour -> three.js linear working colour
function unlit(hex: string): MeshBasicMaterial;          // flat colour, no lighting
function boxMesh(size: Vec3, material: Material): Mesh;  // full edge lengths along x, y, z
function sphereMesh(radius: number, material: Material, segments = 32, rings = 16): Mesh;
function lookAtCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; fovY?: number /* radians, full vertical, default 0.9 */; near?: number /* 0.1 */; far?: number /* 1000 */ }): PerspectiveCamera;  // square aspect
function orthographicCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; height?: number /* visible world height = width, default 10 */; near?: number; far?: number }): OrthographicCamera;
function startTask(build: (host: TaskHost) => TaskApp | Promise<TaskApp>): Promise<void>;

interface TaskHost {
  onKeyDown(code: string, handler: () => void): void;   // after the key went down
  onKeyUp(code: string, handler: () => void): void;     // after the key went up
  isKeyDown(code: string): boolean;                     // as of the current frame
  onInput(name: string, handler: (value: unknown) => void): void; // declares a host input; the page sets it, the handler gets the value in the next frame's input phase
}
interface TaskApp {
  readonly scene: Scene;
  readonly camera: Camera;
  readonly clearColor: string;                          // "#rrggbb" (sRGB)
  fixedUpdate?(dt: number): void;                       // once per fixed tick, dt = 1/60
  update?(dt: number): void;                            // once per frame, dt in seconds (clamped to 0.1)
}

// Textures (an image the project provides as assets/<name>, loaded before the scene is built):
function loadTexture(url: string, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear" /* default srgb */; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): Promise<Texture>;
function configureTexture<T extends Texture>(texture: T, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear"; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): T;
// build may be async: `void startTask(async (host) => { const t = await loadTexture("assets/swatch.png", { filter: "nearest", wrap: "repeat" }); ... })`
```

The camera helpers and primitives use the defaults above; plain three.js objects work as well.

## three.js r186 essentials

Units are metres and radians; the coordinate system is right-handed with +Y up, the camera looks down -Z until it is
told otherwise; colours given as `"#rrggbb"` or hex numbers are sRGB and are converted to the linear working space
(`new Color(0x22c55e)`, `new Color().setStyle("#22c55e")`, or `srgb("#22c55e")`).

**Scene graph.** `Object3D` (base of `Scene`, `Group`, `Mesh`, lights, cameras): `name`, `position` (`Vector3`: `set(x,y,z)`,
`x`, `y`, `z`), `rotation` (`Euler`, radians, order XYZ: `rotation.y += a`), `quaternion`, `scale` (`Vector3`), `visible`,
`add(...children)`, `remove(...children)`, `children`, `parent`, `getObjectByName(name)`, `traverse(fn)`,
`lookAt(x, y, z)`, `rotateX/Y/Z(angle)`. A child's transform is relative to its parent; `new Group()` is an empty
node used to move several objects together.

**Meshes and geometry.** `new Mesh(geometry, material)`. Geometries (all dimensions are full sizes unless it says radius):
`BoxGeometry(width, height, depth)`, `SphereGeometry(radius, widthSegments = 32, heightSegments = 16)`,
`PlaneGeometry(width, height)` (lies in the XY plane facing +Z; `rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2` lays it flat facing +Y),
`CylinderGeometry(radiusTop, radiusBottom, height, radialSegments)`, `ConeGeometry(radius, height, radialSegments)`,
`CircleGeometry(radius, segments)`, `TorusGeometry(radius, tube, radialSegments, tubularSegments)`.

**Materials.** `MeshBasicMaterial({ color, map?, side? })`: unlit flat colour. `MeshStandardMaterial({ color, roughness,
metalness, map? })`: physically based, needs lights. `material.color` is a `Color` (`material.color.set("#ff0000")`,
`.copy(srgb("#ff0000"))`, `.setRGB(r, g, b)` in linear values); `material.name` is a string; `material.map` a `Texture`;
`material.side` is `FrontSide` (default), `BackSide` or `DoubleSide`. A material is shared by every mesh that uses it.
Changing `color` of a built material takes effect on the next frame; nothing has to be rebuilt.

**Lights** (physical units): `AmbientLight(color, intensity)`; `DirectionalLight(color, intensity)` shines from its
`position` toward its `target` (default the origin); `PointLight(color, intensity, distance = 0, decay = 2)` with
`distance` 0 meaning no range limit; `SpotLight`, `HemisphereLight` exist too. A matte surface of colour `albedo` facing a
point light of intensity `I` at distance `d` (decay 2) has the outgoing radiance `albedo * I / (pi * d * d)`; a surface
facing a directional light of intensity `E` squarely has `albedo * E / pi`; ambient light adds `albedo * intensity / pi`
(each multiplied by the light colour). Lights are `Object3D`s: add them to the scene.

**Cameras.** `PerspectiveCamera(fovDegrees, aspect, near, far)` (field of view in DEGREES, vertical), `OrthographicCamera(left, right,
top, bottom, near, far)`; place with `position.set(...)` and `lookAt(...)`.

**Math.** `Vector3` (`set`, `add`, `sub`, `multiplyScalar`, `length`, `normalize`, `lerp`, `clone`), `Color`, `Euler`,
`Quaternion` (`setFromAxisAngle(axis, angle)`), `MathUtils.degToRad`, `MathUtils.clamp`, `MathUtils.lerp`, `MathUtils.mapLinear`.

## TSL (`three/tsl`): shader logic as node expressions

A node material replaces fixed material parameters by node graphs; the shader is built once when the material is first
used, so animate through uniforms, not by replacing the material.

```ts
import { uniform, vec3, color, mix, sin, positionLocal, uv, texture, float, clamp, smoothstep } from "three/tsl";
import { MeshBasicNodeMaterial, MeshStandardNodeMaterial } from "three/webgpu";

const level = uniform(0.25);                 // a node with a mutable `.value` (number, Color, Vector3, ...)
const material = new MeshBasicNodeMaterial(); // unlit; MeshStandardNodeMaterial for lit materials
material.name = "Shade";
material.colorNode = vec3(level);            // per-pixel colour; the result is displayed as it is
level.value = 0.5;                           // updates the shader's input, no rebuild
```

- Constructors: `float(x)`, `vec2(...)`, `vec3(...)` (`vec3(s)` fills all three), `vec4(...)`, `color(colorOrHex)`.
- Arithmetic on nodes: `a.add(b)`, `a.sub(b)`, `a.mul(b)`, `a.div(b)`, `a.oneMinus()`, `a.negate()`; numbers are accepted
  where a node is expected. Components: `v.x`, `v.y`, `v.z`, `v.xyz`.
- Functions (each also a method): `mix(a, b, t)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `smoothstep(lo, hi, x)`, `step(edge, x)`, `sin`, `cos`,
  `abs`, `pow`, `fract`, `min`, `max`, `length`, `normalize`, `dot`, `saturate`.
- Inputs: `positionLocal` (object-space position of the surface point, a vec3), `positionWorld`, `normalLocal`,
  `normalWorld`, `uv()` (texture coordinates, a vec2), `texture(tex, uv?)` (a sampled vec4), `time` (seconds of the
  renderer's own real-time clock, not of the application's frame clock).
- Node material slots: `colorNode` (base colour; for `MeshBasicNodeMaterial` the final colour), `opacityNode`, `roughnessNode`,
  `metalnessNode`, `emissiveNode` (on `MeshStandardNodeMaterial`).
- `color(c)` makes a colour node from a three.js `Color` (for an sRGB hex colour pass `srgb("#rrggbb")`). Node arithmetic on
  colours is done in linear light, and the result is displayed as it is.
- Conditionals: `select(condition, a, b)`; `If(cond, () => { ... })` inside `Fn(() => { ... })`.

## Conventions of the tests

Tests press keys, set host inputs, step frames of a given duration and compare pixels of the render target with
colours. Nothing else is observable: motion shows as pixels, state shows as colours. A project that does not type-check,
throws on start or writes to the console (errors or warnings) fails.

# Task: A tilted amber bar with a red ball at its end

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #101820.
- One camera at (0, 0, 8) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 100).
- An amber box named Bar centred at the origin: colour #f59e0b, edge length 4.0 along its own x axis, 1.0 along its own y axis and 0.5 along its own z axis. It is rotated about the world Z axis by 0.9272952 radians, counter-clockwise as seen from the camera (the angle whose cosine is 0.6 and whose sine is 0.8), so that its own x axis points along (0.6, 0.8, 0).
- A red sphere named Tip at (1.2, 1.6, 0), which is the middle of the end face of the bar that lies along its own +x axis: colour #ef4444, radius 0.6.
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These objects must exist when you are done, each with a three.js `name` (or material `name`) equal to the identifier: Bar, Tip

# Reference documentation (three.js r186 and the project's support module)

# Reference: three.js r186 (WebGPU, TSL) and the project's support module

This document is the same for every task. It lists the API a project can rely on; every name in it was checked
against the installed packages (three 0.186.1).

## How a project works

The project is TypeScript (`strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) with one entry, `src/main.ts`, bundled for a browser.
It imports three.js from `three/webgpu` (all classes) and `three/tsl` (the node shading language) and the support module
from `@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`. The entry calls `startTask` exactly once:

```ts
import { Scene } from "three/webgpu";
import { boxMesh, lookAtCamera, startTask, unlit } from "@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support";

void startTask((host) => {
  const scene = new Scene();
  const cube = boxMesh([1, 1, 1], unlit("#22c55e"));
  cube.name = "Cube";
  scene.add(cube);
  host.onKeyDown("Space", () => { /* runs in the input phase of the next frame */ });
  return {
    scene,
    camera: lookAtCamera({ position: [0, 0, 6], target: [0, 0, 0] }),
    clearColor: "#202020",
    update(dt) { cube.rotation.y += dt; },
  };
});
```

`startTask` owns the renderer, a square 128 x 128 sRGB render target and the clock. Tests drive the application
frame by frame; the picture they read is the render target. A frame runs in this order: host inputs, key
transitions (down/up handlers), fixed ticks (`fixedUpdate`, 0 to 4 per frame of 1/60 s each), `update(dt)`, then the
render. Keys are named by `KeyboardEvent.code` (`"Space"`, `"KeyA"`, `"Enter"`, `"ArrowLeft"`).

Objects the task names are found by their `name` property (`mesh.name = "Cube"`, `material.name = "Sweep"`); give each
named thing exactly the name the task uses.

## The support module (`@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`)

```ts
type Vec3 = readonly [number, number, number];
function srgb(hex: string): Color;                       // "#rrggbb" sRGB colour -> three.js linear working colour
function unlit(hex: string): MeshBasicMaterial;          // flat colour, no lighting
function boxMesh(size: Vec3, material: Material): Mesh;  // full edge lengths along x, y, z
function sphereMesh(radius: number, material: Material, segments = 32, rings = 16): Mesh;
function lookAtCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; fovY?: number /* radians, full vertical, default 0.9 */; near?: number /* 0.1 */; far?: number /* 1000 */ }): PerspectiveCamera;  // square aspect
function orthographicCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; height?: number /* visible world height = width, default 10 */; near?: number; far?: number }): OrthographicCamera;
function startTask(build: (host: TaskHost) => TaskApp | Promise<TaskApp>): Promise<void>;

interface TaskHost {
  onKeyDown(code: string, handler: () => void): void;   // after the key went down
  onKeyUp(code: string, handler: () => void): void;     // after the key went up
  isKeyDown(code: string): boolean;                     // as of the current frame
  onInput(name: string, handler: (value: unknown) => void): void; // declares a host input; the page sets it, the handler gets the value in the next frame's input phase
}
interface TaskApp {
  readonly scene: Scene;
  readonly camera: Camera;
  readonly clearColor: string;                          // "#rrggbb" (sRGB)
  fixedUpdate?(dt: number): void;                       // once per fixed tick, dt = 1/60
  update?(dt: number): void;                            // once per frame, dt in seconds (clamped to 0.1)
}

// Textures (an image the project provides as assets/<name>, loaded before the scene is built):
function loadTexture(url: string, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear" /* default srgb */; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): Promise<Texture>;
function configureTexture<T extends Texture>(texture: T, o: { colorSpace?: "srgb" | "linear"; filter: "nearest" | "linear"; wrap: "repeat" | "clamp" }): T;
// build may be async: `void startTask(async (host) => { const t = await loadTexture("assets/swatch.png", { filter: "nearest", wrap: "repeat" }); ... })`
```

The camera helpers and primitives use the defaults above; plain three.js objects work as well.

## three.js r186 essentials

Units are metres and radians; the coordinate system is right-handed with +Y up, the camera looks down -Z until it is
told otherwise; colours given as `"#rrggbb"` or hex numbers are sRGB and are converted to the linear working space
(`new Color(0x22c55e)`, `new Color().setStyle("#22c55e")`, or `srgb("#22c55e")`).

**Scene graph.** `Object3D` (base of `Scene`, `Group`, `Mesh`, lights, cameras): `name`, `position` (`Vector3`: `set(x,y,z)`,
`x`, `y`, `z`), `rotation` (`Euler`, radians, order XYZ: `rotation.y += a`), `quaternion`, `scale` (`Vector3`), `visible`,
`add(...children)`, `remove(...children)`, `children`, `parent`, `getObjectByName(name)`, `traverse(fn)`,
`lookAt(x, y, z)`, `rotateX/Y/Z(angle)`. A child's transform is relative to its parent; `new Group()` is an empty
node used to move several objects together.

**Meshes and geometry.** `new Mesh(geometry, material)`. Geometries (all dimensions are full sizes unless it says radius):
`BoxGeometry(width, height, depth)`, `SphereGeometry(radius, widthSegments = 32, heightSegments = 16)`,
`PlaneGeometry(width, height)` (lies in the XY plane facing +Z; `rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2` lays it flat facing +Y),
`CylinderGeometry(radiusTop, radiusBottom, height, radialSegments)`, `ConeGeometry(radius, height, radialSegments)`,
`CircleGeometry(radius, segments)`, `TorusGeometry(radius, tube, radialSegments, tubularSegments)`.

**Materials.** `MeshBasicMaterial({ color, map?, side? })`: unlit flat colour. `MeshStandardMaterial({ color, roughness,
metalness, map? })`: physically based, needs lights. `material.color` is a `Color` (`material.color.set("#ff0000")`,
`.copy(srgb("#ff0000"))`, `.setRGB(r, g, b)` in linear values); `material.name` is a string; `material.map` a `Texture`;
`material.side` is `FrontSide` (default), `BackSide` or `DoubleSide`. A material is shared by every mesh that uses it.
Changing `color` of a built material takes effect on the next frame; nothing has to be rebuilt.

**Lights** (physical units): `AmbientLight(color, intensity)`; `DirectionalLight(color, intensity)` shines from its
`position` toward its `target` (default the origin); `PointLight(color, intensity, distance = 0, decay = 2)` with
`distance` 0 meaning no range limit; `SpotLight`, `HemisphereLight` exist too. A matte surface of colour `albedo` facing a
point light of intensity `I` at distance `d` (decay 2) has the outgoing radiance `albedo * I / (pi * d * d)`; a surface
facing a directional light of intensity `E` squarely has `albedo * E / pi`; ambient light adds `albedo * intensity / pi`
(each multiplied by the light colour). Lights are `Object3D`s: add them to the scene.

**Cameras.** `PerspectiveCamera(fovDegrees, aspect, near, far)` (field of view in DEGREES, vertical), `OrthographicCamera(left, right,
top, bottom, near, far)`; place with `position.set(...)` and `lookAt(...)`.

**Math.** `Vector3` (`set`, `add`, `sub`, `multiplyScalar`, `length`, `normalize`, `lerp`, `clone`), `Color`, `Euler`,
`Quaternion` (`setFromAxisAngle(axis, angle)`), `MathUtils.degToRad`, `MathUtils.clamp`, `MathUtils.lerp`, `MathUtils.mapLinear`.

## TSL (`three/tsl`): shader logic as node expressions

A node material replaces fixed material parameters by node graphs; the shader is built once when the material is first
used, so animate through uniforms, not by replacing the material.

```ts
import { uniform, vec3, color, mix, sin, positionLocal, uv, texture, float, clamp, smoothstep } from "three/tsl";
import { MeshBasicNodeMaterial, MeshStandardNodeMaterial } from "three/webgpu";

const level = uniform(0.25);                 // a node with a mutable `.value` (number, Color, Vector3, ...)
const material = new MeshBasicNodeMaterial(); // unlit; MeshStandardNodeMaterial for lit materials
material.name = "Shade";
material.colorNode = vec3(level);            // per-pixel colour; the result is displayed as it is
level.value = 0.5;                           // updates the shader's input, no rebuild
```

- Constructors: `float(x)`, `vec2(...)`, `vec3(...)` (`vec3(s)` fills all three), `vec4(...)`, `color(colorOrHex)`.
- Arithmetic on nodes: `a.add(b)`, `a.sub(b)`, `a.mul(b)`, `a.div(b)`, `a.oneMinus()`, `a.negate()`; numbers are accepted
  where a node is expected. Components: `v.x`, `v.y`, `v.z`, `v.xyz`.
- Functions (each also a method): `mix(a, b, t)`, `clamp(x, lo, hi)`, `smoothstep(lo, hi, x)`, `step(edge, x)`, `sin`, `cos`,
  `abs`, `pow`, `fract`, `min`, `max`, `length`, `normalize`, `dot`, `saturate`.
- Inputs: `positionLocal` (object-space position of the surface point, a vec3), `positionWorld`, `normalLocal`,
  `normalWorld`, `uv()` (texture coordinates, a vec2), `texture(tex, uv?)` (a sampled vec4), `time` (seconds of the
  renderer's own real-time clock, not of the application's frame clock).
- Node material slots: `colorNode` (base colour; for `MeshBasicNodeMaterial` the final colour), `opacityNode`, `roughnessNode`,
  `metalnessNode`, `emissiveNode` (on `MeshStandardNodeMaterial`).
- `color(c)` makes a colour node from a three.js `Color` (for an sRGB hex colour pass `srgb("#rrggbb")`). Node arithmetic on
  colours is done in linear light, and the result is displayed as it is.
- Conditionals: `select(condition, a, b)`; `If(cond, () => { ... })` inside `Fn(() => { ... })`.

## Conventions of the tests

Tests press keys, set host inputs, step frames of a given duration and compare pixels of the render target with
colours. Nothing else is observable: motion shows as pixels, state shows as colours. A project that does not type-check,
throws on start or writes to the console (errors or warnings) fails.

# Task: A two-segment arm built as a hierarchy of nodes

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #14161c.
- One camera at (0, 0, 9) looking at the origin, with a perspective projection (vertical field of view 0.8 radians, near plane 0.1, far plane 1000).
- A grey box named Base at (-2.5, -1.5, 0): colour #64748b, edge length 1.2.
- An arm made of nodes in a hierarchy. Every position, rotation and scale below is given relative to the node's PARENT, so a child moves, turns and scales with its parent. Rotations are counter-clockwise about the Z axis as seen from the camera, in radians.
  - Arm: a node with no shape at (-2.5, -1.5, 0), rotated by 0.6435011 (cosine 0.8, sine 0.6), scale 1. Its children:
    - Upper: a box named Upper at (2, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, colour #3b82f6, edge lengths 4.0 along its own x axis, 0.8 along y and 0.6 along z.
    - Elbow: a node with no shape at (4, 0, 0) in the Arm's frame, rotated by -1.287002, uniform scale 0.75. Its children:
      - Fore: a box named Fore at (1.5, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #22c55e, edge lengths 3.0 x 0.7 x 0.5 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
      - Hand: a sphere named Hand at (3, 0, 0) in the Elbow's frame, colour #f43f5e, radius 0.6 (before the Elbow's scale applies).
All surfaces are flat colours (no lighting).

These declarations must exist when you are done: Demo.Base, Demo.Arm, Demo.Arm.Upper, Demo.Arm.Elbow, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Fore, Demo.Arm.Elbow.Hand

Build a scene named Demo that renders exactly as follows. The picture is square.
- The clear (background) colour is #14161c.

# Reference documentation (three.js r186 and the project's support module)

# Reference: three.js r186 (WebGPU, TSL) and the project's support module

This document is the same for every task. It lists the API a project can rely on; every name in it was checked
against the installed packages (three 0.186.1).

## How a project works

The project is TypeScript (`strict`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) with one entry, `src/main.ts`, bundled for a browser.
It imports three.js from `three/webgpu` (all classes) and `three/tsl` (the node shading language) and the support module
from `@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`. The entry calls `startTask` exactly once:

```ts
import { Scene } from "three/webgpu";
import { boxMesh, lookAtCamera, startTask, unlit } from "@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support";

void startTask((host) => {
  const scene = new Scene();
  const cube = boxMesh([1, 1, 1], unlit("#22c55e"));
  cube.name = "Cube";
  scene.add(cube);
  host.onKeyDown("Space", () => { /* runs in the input phase of the next frame */ });
  return {
    scene,
    camera: lookAtCamera({ position: [0, 0, 6], target: [0, 0, 0] }),
    clearColor: "#202020",
    update(dt) { cube.rotation.y += dt; },
  };
});
```

`startTask` owns the renderer, a square 128 x 128 sRGB render target and the clock. Tests drive the application
frame by frame; the picture they read is the render target. A frame runs in this order: host inputs, key
transitions (down/up handlers), fixed ticks (`fixedUpdate`, 0 to 4 per frame of 1/60 s each), `update(dt)`, then the
render. Keys are named by `KeyboardEvent.code` (`"Space"`, `"KeyA"`, `"Enter"`, `"ArrowLeft"`).

Objects the task names are found by their `name` property (`mesh.name = "Cube"`, `material.name = "Sweep"`); give each
named thing exactly the name the task uses.

## The support module (`@mtek/benchmarks/baseline-support`)

```ts
type Vec3 = readonly [number, number, number];
function srgb(hex: string): Color;                       // "#rrggbb" sRGB colour -> three.js linear working colour
function unlit(hex: string): MeshBasicMaterial;          // flat colour, no lighting
function boxMesh(size: Vec3, material: Material): Mesh;  // full edge lengths along x, y, z
function sphereMesh(radius: number, material: Material, segments = 32, rings = 16): Mesh;
function lookAtCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; fovY?: number /* radians, full vertical, default 0.9 */; near?: number /* 0.1 */; far?: number /* 1000 */ }): PerspectiveCamera;  // square aspect
function orthographicCamera(o: { position: Vec3; target: Vec3; height?: number /* visible world height = width, default 10 */; near?: number; far?: number }): OrthographicCamera;
function startTask(build: (host: TaskHost) => TaskApp | Promise<TaskApp>): Promise<void>;

interface TaskHost {
  onKeyDown(code: string, handler: () => void): void;   // after the key went down
